prompt: What did the three hosts' first requests show about get_order?

choices.text: That all three APIs share one format, so the hosts sent identical declarations
choices.why: The shapes differ: one flat object, an input_schema, and a tool nested under function.

choices.text: The same tool in three formats
choices.why: Right. One per API: the Responses API, Anthropic's Messages API, and Ollama's /api/chat.

choices.text: That only one host found the tool
choices.why: All three sent it, and all three answered.

choices.text: That MCP rewrote the tool's description
choices.why: The server's description reached all three; one host wrapped it in markers.

prompt: Without a shared protocol, how many adapters do three hosts and two tool providers need?
How did the three hosts get get_order in this lesson?

choices.text: Each copied shop_mcp.py's function into its own code
choices.why: None of them contains a line of get_order.

choices.text: Through a cloud registry that hosts the tool for them
choices.why: The server ran on this machine, started by each host.

choices.text: Through Ollama, which runs the tools itself
choices.why: Ollama is the model provider: it returns a tool call, and the host's client asks the server to run it.

choices.text: Each started the same MCP server and asked it
choices.why: Right. One server, three clients, no change to the server.

prompt: Which connection in this lesson's runs is MCP?

choices.text: The one between each host and Ollama
choices.why: That wire is each provider's own API.

choices.text: Both, since MCP replaces the provider APIs
choices.why: The provider wire stayed in three formats.

choices.text: The one between each host and shop_mcp.py
choices.why: Right. The same whoever the host is; the server never sees the model.

choices.text: Neither; MCP only exists over HTTP
choices.why: These ran over stdio, one of MCP's two transports.

prompt: What does `tee` do in the command hosts.py uses to start the server?

choices.text: It copies what the client writes to the server into a file
choices.why: Right. That copy is what section 04 reads.

choices.text: It filters out messages the server should not see, such as anything larger than a line
choices.why: It passes everything through unchanged.

choices.text: It encrypts the stdio channel
choices.why: tee copies; it does not encrypt.

choices.text: It starts a second server as a backup
choices.why: Only one server runs per host.

prompt: What did the OpenAI SDK's MCP client send first?

choices.text: initialize, with version 2025-11-25, like the other two
choices.why: That was the Claude and Google clients.

choices.text: tools/call, without asking for the list first
choices.why: It listed the tools before calling one.

choices.text: server/discover, with version 2026-07-28
choices.why: Right. No handshake; the version travels on every request.

choices.text: ping
choices.why: ping was removed in 2026-07-28.

prompt: Why could the Claude and Google hosts use a server built with mcp 2.3.0?

choices.text: Because 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28 are the same protocol under two names
choices.why: 2026-07-28 removed the handshake that 2025-11-25 needs.

choices.text: The server is dual-era: it answers legacy and modern clients
choices.why: Right. It answered initialize as well as server/discover.

choices.text: Because their hosts upgraded the server automatically
choices.why: Hosts do not change a server; they connect to it.

choices.text: Because tee translated the messages
choices.why: tee only copies.

prompt: Which primitive is chosen by the person, typically as something like a slash command?

choices.text: Prompts
choices.why: Right. Templates with arguments that a person picks.

choices.text: Tools, which the model asks for and the host allows
choices.why: Tools are asked for by the model.

choices.text: Resources
choices.why: Resources are data the host reads and gives the model.

choices.text: Sampling, the server asking the client's model for text
choices.why: Sampling is a client feature, and deprecated in 2026-07-28.

prompt: Which features does the 2026-07-28 revision list as deprecated? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Roots
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Sampling
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Tools
choices.why: Tools are a core primitive.

choices.text: The HTTP+SSE transport
choices.why: Right. Streamable HTTP replaces it.

choices.text: The stdio transport
choices.why: stdio is one of the two transports.

prompt: In the 2026-07-28 revision, how does a server get a confirmation from the person in the middle of a request?

choices.text: It sends its own request to the client over a connection kept open
choices.why: That was how earlier revisions did it.

choices.text: It waits until the client calls server/discover again
choices.why: server/discover advertises versions and capabilities; it carries no answers.

choices.text: It cannot; MCP has no way to ask
choices.why: Multi round-trip requests are that way.

choices.text: It returns an input_required result, and the client retries with the answers
choices.why: Right. That is a multi round-trip request.

prompt: Why did the Claude host's model see mcp__shop__get_order while the others saw get_order?

choices.text: Because the server named it differently for each client
choices.why: The server sent the same tool list to all three.

choices.text: That choice belongs to whoever embeds the client, not the protocol
choices.why: Right. Prefixing keeps two servers' tools apart; MCP leaves it to the host.

choices.text: Because Anthropic's API requires a prefix on every tool
choices.why: Lesson 4's tools reached the Messages API without one.

choices.text: Because the 2025-11-25 revision renames tools
choices.why: Revisions do not rename tools; the Google host used the same revision and kept the name.

prompt: What did the Google host do with the server's tool description?

choices.text: Deleted it, sending only the name
choices.why: The description was there, between markers.

choices.text: Translated it into the model's language
choices.why: The text was unchanged.

choices.text: Wrapped it between markers that label it untrusted
choices.why: Right. It tells the model whose words those are; it does not make it ignore them.

choices.text: Checked it against a list of approved descriptions kept by Google
choices.why: No list was consulted; the text was wrapped and sent.

When is an in-process function tool the better choice than an MCP server?

choices.text: When the tool belongs to another team that changes it often
choices.why: That is a reason for a server, not against one.

choices.text: When the person chooses which tools to install
choices.why: That is what made MCP common.

choices.text: When the tool must run next to a database under its own account
choices.why: A remote server is how that is done.

choices.text: One agent owns its tools
choices.why: Right. A server adds a process, a protocol and a boundary for nothing.

prompt: Why is a remote server also a security argument?

choices.text: Because remote servers cannot be prompted
choices.why: Their descriptions still reach the model.

choices.text: It runs with exactly the access it needs, under its own account, not the host's
choices.why: Right. Least privilege drawn as a process boundary.

choices.text: Because HTTP is encrypted and stdio is not
choices.why: Encryption is a transport detail; the argument is about access.

choices.text: Because its vendor reviews its descriptions first
choices.why: Nothing guarantees that.
